course_title: Tort Claims Against Government - Private Remedies for Public Wrongs
course_description:
Provides an in-depth study of the ways in which tort law ensures accountability and compensates for injury caused by the wrongful use of state powers. Covers state immunity, misfeasance in public office, false imprisonment, and public body negligence in key areas of social regulation and welfare provision such as policing, public health and safety, immigration detention and the protection of the mentally ill.

Tort Claims Against Government - Private Remedies for Public Wrongs ﾠ

This course examines the tort liability of Government and public bodies. In practice, the State is now a popular defendant in civil claims of all sorts, not just because it is always solvent and has ‘deep pockets’, but also because of its increased intrusion into private lives resulting from ever-higher levels of social regulation. Since the growth of the 'administrative state' through the twentieth century, public bodies and officials have come to be engaged in regulating a very wide range of human conduct and in providing a wide range of services from roads, to policing, fire services, mental health provision, child protection, prisons, immigration, and environmental regulation. In recent times in particular, the capacity of the State to carry out all of these functions efficiently and competently has been compromised by serious constraints on public finance as, well, sometimes, as by a lack of political will.

The course examines the history of Crown immunities in tort, the special reasons for treating public actors differently from private defendants and some of the most significant tortious causes of action that regulate wrongful exercises of (or failures to exercise) public power. We look at the torts of misfeasance in public office, false imprisonment, and the tort of negligence (with special reference to the negligence liability of the police, child protection agencies, prison and immigration authorities, health authorities and local councils). We also look in detail at the raft of legislative reforms that have been introduced in the wake of the Ipp Review into the law of Negligence in 2001, the effect of which is to attempt significantly to curtail the civil liability of public bodies exercising specialised statutory functions and to introduce new forms of immunity. And we consider the implications for State responsibilities of the appearance in Australia of domestic Human Rights legislation. The course is a case-law-focussed course; in this respect methodologically much like the law of Torts 2, but it also requires greater attention to overlaps between public and private law; and between the common law and statutory provisions and purposes. It also delves in depth into some of the difficult social contexts in which public body decision-making is made - from the treatment of mental health issues and suicide in the community, to police and other public agency responses to child abuse, to the use of state force to imprison refugees seeking asylum from persecution or violence.

There are no lectures. Students are firmly expected to read the provided materials in advance, guided by a short, recorded overview of the main issues. It is through interactive face-to-face seminars (which are not recorded ) and is assessed entirely through independent research components. The focus is on stimulating students to read extensively, conduct their own research work and then to present the results of this research in writing. They are invited through these techniques to formulate their own perspectives on the relationship between tort law and the State.

Some of the seminars will be co-led by His Honour, Justice James Edelman of the High Court of Australia . Guest experts are also invited to lead discussion on particular topics such as immigration detention and climate change litigation.

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

Course Aims

The aim of this courseﾠis to provide a structuredﾠframework through which students may develop their own understanding of the nature, basis and scope of public body liability in tort in the modern day through their own independent reading and research. There are no formal lectures.ﾠSeminars are focussed on structured identification and discussion of key issues, student presentations and problem-solving activities, often conducted in teams.

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate detailed knowledge of the principles governing the tortious liability of public authorities for malicious prosecution, misfeasance in public office, false imprisonment and negligence (with a particular focus on the negligence liability of the police, child-protection agencies, prison and health authorities and local councils).
Demonstrate advanced problem-solving skills within the field.
Demonstrate advanced, independent research-skills within the field, including the ability to locate and reference materials beyond those provided, through use of libraries and on-line databases.
Demonstrate ability to communicate ideas and research findings effectively in writing and to observe disciplinary citation practices.

assessment_details.title: Problem Solving Exercise
assessment_details.task_description: This written problem-solving exercise will span the course syllabus, testing your understanding of the various topics and your ability to research and apply the relevant principles to a novel set of facts. It involves the conduct of independent research of the law, as well as the application of that law to advise a client about a concrete set of facts. Read full task description Hide full task description
assessment_details.assessment_security: Open assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking.
assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Detailed submission guidelines will be provided via blackboard closer to the submission date.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 7 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Extension to Assessment Due Date
The maximum extension for an assessment item due within the semester / teaching period in which the course is offered is 7 days. In exceptional circumstances, an extension may be approved for a further 7 days. Where a student is incapacitated for a period longer than 14 days, they are advised to apply for removal of course.
A student may apply for an extension to assessment due date if they are unable to meet an assessment deadline due to extenuating circumstances. Please refer to the Applying for an extension page on my.UQ for further details on acceptable reasons for an extension and for instructions on how to apply . Additional information on extensions can be found within the Assessment Procedure .
Spoken or written notification of difficulties with assessment deadlines to a course coordinator or the School does not constitute an authorised extension.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Penalties for Late Submission
The following penalties apply to late submission of an assessment item, assuming that an extension has not been approved, and that late submission is academically possible (e.g., it does not delay feedback to a cohort, or interfere with course delivery).
First 7 periods of 24 hours (or part thereof) - 10% per 24 hours of the maximum possible mark for the assessment item. For example, a report worth a maximum of 40 marks, submitted 28 hours late will attract a penalty of 8 marks, calculated as 2 periods of 24 hours x 10% x 40 marks.
More than 7 periods of 24 hours - 100%.

assessment_details.other_conditions: Time limited, Secure. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: You will be examined in a closed book format on two research essay topics chosen from a list of pre-defined topics made available in advance of the examination. The topics are to be researched in advance, using the course materials as a starting point but then also referring to further materials and arguments gathered independently through the use of library and on-line research resources databases. Essays in the examination will distil and present considered research findings on the topics in question under secure conditions. The purpose of this format is to enable students to engage in depth with material that is of particular interest to them in order to develop higher levels of insight and understanding than is customarily possible in a closed book examination format. A total of two essays must be completed during the examination. Each essay carries equal marks. Read full task description Hide full task description

You must only use the approved materials and tools for this assessment task. Use of prohibited materials in this task may be investigated and treated as academic misconduct. See assessment instructions for more details.
